abstract: The way that laboratory rodents are handled has a significant impact on their welfare. Picking up mice by the tail increases anxiety, reduces voluntary interaction with handlers, and reduces behavioural test reliability compared to more refined handling methods, such as picking up mice inside a handling tunnel or cupping freely on the hand. An alternative in use by the community is to restrain a mouse by the tail-base while scooping it up on the hand and supporting its weight (tail-cup method). Here, we assess whether tail-cup handling is a welfare refinement compared to picking up mice by tail or tunnel, using both sexes of two strains (BALB/c, C57BL/6). Tail-cup handling reduced aversion to interact with the handler compared to tail handling, but to a much smaller extent than tunnel handling. Tail-cup and tunnel handling both reduced anxiety in an elevated plus maze relative to tail-handled mice. However, test reliability was substantially better using tunnel handling in a habituation-dishabituation task, greatly reducing numbers of animals required for testing. These findings generalised across sexes and strains tested. While tail-cup handling provides some improvement over traditional tail handling, tunnel handling appears to be more beneficial for mouse welfare and behavioural reliability.

summary: Compares tail-cup, tail, and tunnel handling of mice; tunnel handling best improved welfare and behavioural test reliability across sexes and strains.
title: The impact of tail-cup handling as an alternative method for picking up laboratory mice
